stem:
A 24-year-old woman is brought to ED by ambulance one hour after ingesting an unknown number of amitriptyline 25 mg tablets from her partner's supply. She is drowsy but rousable to voice. Her pupils are dilated at 6 mm bilaterally with sluggish reaction, and her skin is warm and dry.

Her partner reports the bottle held approximately sixty tablets three days ago and is now empty. There is no history of coingestion or alcohol use. She has a background of adjustment disorder but no prior overdoses.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 37.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, GCS 12; pupils 6 mm sluggish; warm dry skin; bowel sounds absent; urinary retention present
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus tachycardia rate 128, QRS 128 milliseconds, terminal R in aVR of 4 mm; VBG pH 7.32, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 3.6 mmol/L, glucose 6.2 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus repeated to QRS narrowing
options.rationale: QRS above 100 ms in TCA overdose is an indication for sodium bicarbonate bolus targeting pH 7.5 and QRS narrowing; reverses fast sodium channel blockade. (Source: eTG: Toxicology; ACEM Poison guidelines)

options.text: Intravenous physostigmine 0.5 to 2 mg over 3 minutes to reverse anticholinergic toxidrome
options.rationale: Physostigmine is contraindicated in TCA overdose because it increases risk of seizures and asystole; sodium bicarbonate is the priority. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Intravenous flumazenil 0.2 mg titrated to reverse suspected sedative co-ingestion
options.rationale: Flumazenil precipitates seizures particularly in mixed overdoses and pro-convulsant coingestants like TCA; not indicated here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g bolus for arrhythmia prevention and rate control
options.rationale: Magnesium is used for torsades but does not treat sodium channel blockade; sodium bicarbonate is the mechanism-directed antidote. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

options.text: Intravenous lignocaine loading 1 mg/kg followed by infusion at 1 to 4 mg/min
options.rationale: Lignocaine also blocks sodium channels and compounds TCA toxicity; contraindicated as first-line arrhythmia treatment in TCA. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

explanation.summary: TCA overdose combines anticholinergic toxidrome, sodium channel blockade (widening QRS, terminal R in aVR, hypotension) and alpha-1 blockade. Sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg IV bolus is the mechanism-directed antidote for QRS above 100 ms or hypotension unresponsive to fluids, targeting pH 7.45 to 7.55. Seizures are treated with benzodiazepines; refractory hypotension with noradrenaline. Physostigmine is contraindicated. Terminal R wave 3 mm or more in aVR predicts cardiotoxicity. Intralipid emulsion is a rescue option for cardiovascular collapse.
key_points: QRS 100 ms or more or terminal R in aVR 3 mm or more predicts TCA toxicity.
Sodium bicarbonate 1 to 2 mmol/kg bolus is first-line.
Target pH 7.45 to 7.55; narrow QRS as endpoint.
Physostigmine contraindicated; benzodiazepines for seizures.
explanation.pearls: TCA overdose with QRS above 100 ms: 1 to 2 mmol/kg IV sodium bicarbonate boluses to pH 7.5 or QRS narrowing; physostigmine is a contraindication.

stem:
A 27-year-old woman presents to a GP saying that she thinks she may have ADHD after her nephew was recently diagnosed. She reports lifelong difficulty finishing tasks, losing keys and wallet, chronic lateness, and needing to reread paragraphs. She dropped out of university in second year and has changed jobs six times.

She has no history of substance use, no mood disorder currently, and no previous psychiatric admissions. She holds a manual car licence and commutes 45 minutes to work daily. Her PHQ-9 today is 6 and GAD-7 is 5. She asks whether she can start medication urgently.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 80/min, blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, engaged; no thought disorder; euthymic; no tics or motor abnormalities
data_table.Investigations: PHQ-9 6, GAD-7 5, ASRS-6 positive on 5 of 6 items; TSH 1.6 mIU/L; ferritin 48 mcg/L; iron studies within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Trial atomoxetine 40 mg oral daily now under the GP; review at four weeks
options.rationale: Atomoxetine can be initiated by GP under an authority prescription only for confirmed ADHD; diagnosis has not yet been made. (Source: RACGP; RANZCP ADHD Guideline)

options.text: Refer to a psychiatrist for structured adult ADHD assessment before any medication trial
options.rationale: Adult ADHD diagnosis in AU requires psychiatrist assessment for stimulant authorisation; GP self-management is not permitted first-line. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guideline; state stimulant authority rules)

options.text: Trial methylphenidate immediate release 10 mg BD from the GP with driving advice
options.rationale: Stimulants require state-based authority prescriber (usually psychiatrist) for adult initiation; GP alone cannot start. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guideline)

options.text: Recommend cognitive behavioural therapy alone for eight sessions before considering medication
options.rationale: CBT is a helpful adjunct but should not delay assessment and treatment when functional impairment is established. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guideline)

options.text: Advise this is likely age-appropriate distractibility; reassure and review in six months
options.rationale: Reassurance in the presence of impairment across educational, occupational and daily life domains misses a diagnosable condition. (Source: RANZCP Adult ADHD Guideline)

explanation.summary: Adult ADHD in Australia requires psychiatrist (or paediatrician for those under 18) assessment for diagnosis and stimulant authorisation. GP shared care can continue treatment once initiated. Assessment includes DSM-5 criteria (five of nine inattentive or hyperactive-impulsive symptoms persisting over 6 months with impairment in more than one setting, onset before age 12 by history), collateral where possible, and comorbid mood, anxiety, learning disorder screening. Treatment options include long-acting methylphenidate or lisdexamfetamine; atomoxetine and guanfacine are non-stimulant options. Driving advice: patients must self-report medical conditions affecting driving; stimulants generally improve driving safety once titrated, but untreated ADHD is associated with elevated crash risk.
key_points: Adult ADHD diagnosis by psychiatrist required for stimulants in AU.
GP shared care after psychiatrist initiation.
Onset before age 12 by history required for DSM-5.
Driving safer with treated than untreated ADHD.
explanation.pearls: For suspected adult ADHD, refer to a psychiatrist first; state stimulant authorities preclude GP-only initiation, but GP shared care can continue treatment once established.

stem:
A 28-year-old man with schizoaffective disorder is brought to ED by family after four days of progressive withdrawal, mutism, and staying frozen in unusual postures. On the ward he has been observed to hold an arm in mid-air after physical positioning by the nurse and repeats phrases spoken to him. He has not eaten or drunk in 36 hours.

He was on aripiprazole 15 mg daily until two weeks ago when he self-ceased. He has had no antipsychotics since. His mother reports he had a similar episode two years ago that resolved with ECT after an unsuccessful medication trial.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108/min, blood pressure 108/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 37.1 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Mute, waxy flexibility on limb positioning, echolalia, staring; no rigidity or tremor; no autonomic instability
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 320 U/L (below 200); electrolytes within normal limits; venous blood gas within normal limits; CT brain normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate diagnostic and initial treatment step?

options.text: Recommence aripiprazole 30 mg oral daily targeting rapid remission of psychosis
options.rationale: Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia and precipitate neuroleptic malignant syndrome; benzodiazepine challenge first. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; RANZCP catatonia)

options.text: Commence olanzapine 10 mg intramuscular now for rapid tranquillisation of psychosis
options.rationale: IM antipsychotic risks precipitating NMS in catatonia; guideline sequence is lorazepam challenge then ECT if refractory. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Give lorazepam 1 to 2 mg intravenous or intramuscular as a diagnostic and therapeutic challenge
options.rationale: Lorazepam challenge is diagnostic and therapeutic; a 50 percent reduction in catatonia score within 10 minutes confirms diagnosis and guides therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic; RANZCP)

options.text: Refer for emergent ECT under a mental health treatment order today as first therapy
options.rationale: ECT is next-line if lorazepam challenge fails or in malignant catatonia; a lorazepam trial precedes it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Start haloperidol 5 mg oral three times daily and clonazepam 0.5 mg BD together
options.rationale: Haloperidol has the highest NMS risk in catatonia; combination with benzodiazepine does not offset that risk. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Catatonia may present in schizophrenia, mood disorders, delirium, autoimmune encephalitis and other medical conditions. The lorazepam challenge (1 to 2 mg IV or IM) is diagnostic and therapeutic: a marked reduction in Bush Francis Catatonia Rating Scale within 10 minutes confirms diagnosis and guides ongoing treatment (typically lorazepam 2 mg three or four times daily). If two adequate benzodiazepine trials fail, ECT is the next step (also first-line if malignant catatonia with autonomic instability). Antipsychotics can worsen catatonia and precipitate NMS, so they are held during acute treatment.
key_points: Lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IV or IM as challenge test.
50 percent BFCRS reduction confirms diagnosis.
ECT is next-line if benzodiazepines fail.
Withhold antipsychotics acutely to avoid NMS.
explanation.pearls: Suspected catatonia: give lorazepam 1 to 2 mg IV; a rapid response within 10 minutes both confirms diagnosis and treats it, and antipsychotics should be held meanwhile.

stem:
A 35-year-old man is admitted after his third manic episode with psychotic features. On this admission he had elated mood, reduced sleep for a week, grandiose delusions and pressured speech; symptoms resolved within four weeks of olanzapine and mood stabilisation. His two prior episodes were similar and both resolved with treatment.

Between episodes over the past four years he has held a stable job and had good functional recovery. Records show three months of persistent auditory hallucinations after his first admission before eventually resolving during a period of no mood symptoms. He is not currently symptomatic.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76/min, blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Alert, engaged, euthymic; no formal thought disorder currently; no active psychosis on interview
data_table.Investigations: TSH 1.8 mIU/L (within normal limits); serum lithium 0.8 mmol/L (0.6 to 1.0); urine drug screen negative; MRI brain normal

lead_in: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Schizoaffective disorder bipolar type, requiring lifetime mood and antipsychotic combination therapy
options.rationale: Psychosis persisting for two weeks or more outside a mood episode plus mood episodes with psychotic features across illness course meets DSM-5 schizoaffective bipolar type criteria. (Source: DSM-5-TR; RANZCP Bipolar Guidelines)

options.text: Bipolar I disorder with mood congruent psychotic features during the manic episodes only
options.rationale: Bipolar I with psychotic features requires psychosis to be confined to mood episodes; three months of psychosis without mood symptoms excludes this. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Schizophrenia with superimposed mood episodes secondary to reactive depression from illness
options.rationale: Schizophrenia excludes schizoaffective when full mood episodes are present for the majority of illness course; a mood episode dominates here. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Substance-induced mood disorder with psychotic features from prior methamphetamine use
options.rationale: Urine drug screen is negative and episodes recur without substance use; this is not substance induced. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

options.text: Brief psychotic disorder with recurrent depression and mania as separate mood diagnoses
options.rationale: Brief psychotic disorder requires duration less than one month; three months of psychosis excludes this. (Source: DSM-5-TR)

explanation.summary: Schizoaffective disorder requires: (a) an uninterrupted period of illness during which a major mood episode co-occurs with schizophrenia criterion A symptoms; (b) delusions or hallucinations for two or more weeks in the absence of a major mood episode during the lifetime course; (c) mood episodes present for the majority of the total duration of illness (differentiates from schizophrenia); and (d) not attributable to a substance or medical condition. Bipolar type has manic episodes; depressive type has only depression. Management includes long-term mood stabiliser plus antipsychotic (typically lithium plus olanzapine or aripiprazole).
key_points: Schizoaffective needs 2+ weeks of psychosis without mood symptoms in lifetime.
Mood episodes must dominate illness course to differentiate from schizophrenia.
Bipolar type has mania; depressive type only has depression.
Treatment combines mood stabiliser plus antipsychotic.
explanation.pearls: The DSM-5 marker for schizoaffective versus bipolar with psychotic features is 2 weeks or more of psychosis outside any mood episode over the lifetime illness course.

sources.label: RANZCP: Bipolar disorder clinical practice guidelines

stem:
A 52-year-old man with a history of intravenous methamphetamine use presents with three weeks of malaise, drenching night sweats and progressive dyspnoea. He describes cough with intermittent haemoptysis. He has never had rheumatic fever and had no known murmur previously.

He was febrile in triage. Transthoracic echocardiogram in ED shows a 12 mm mobile vegetation on the tricuspid valve with moderate tricuspid regurgitation. Three sets of peripheral blood cultures drawn 30 minutes apart are all positive for Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin sensitive).

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 108/min, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 92 percent on room air, temperature 38.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Pansystolic murmur at left lower sternal edge increasing with inspiration; needle track marks in left cubital fossa; small vasculitic peripheral lesions
data_table.Investigations: Blood cultures 3 of 3 positive Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin sensitive); CRP 240 mg/L (below 5); WCC 18.4 x10^9/L; chest x-ray with bilateral peripheral cavitating nodules

lead_in: How does this case classify under the modified Duke criteria?

options.text: Rejected endocarditis pending transoesophageal echocardiography confirmation
options.rationale: Rejected requires firm alternative diagnosis or resolution with 4 days of antibiotics; this case is not rejected. (Source: BSAC Duke criteria; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Definite endocarditis by two major criteria; empirical benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin therapy
options.rationale: Two major criteria (typical organism in two or more separate cultures plus positive echo with vegetation) equals definite endocarditis; empiric flucloxacillin (or benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin pending sensitivities) is standard. (Source: BSAC Duke criteria; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Possible endocarditis by one major and one minor criterion needing additional imaging
options.rationale: This case fulfils two major criteria, not one; upgraded to definite classification. (Source: BSAC Duke criteria)

options.text: Definite endocarditis by one major and three minor criteria requiring valve replacement
options.rationale: This route is a valid one for definite but not the classification here; two majors already suffice. (Source: BSAC Duke criteria)

options.text: Rejected endocarditis; treat as suspected pulmonary emboli with anticoagulation cover only
options.rationale: The pulmonary nodules represent septic emboli from tricuspid endocarditis, not primary thromboembolic disease. (Source: BSAC Duke criteria)

explanation.summary: The modified Duke criteria define definite endocarditis with either (a) pathological criteria (culture or histology from vegetation or intracardiac abscess); (b) two major clinical criteria; (c) one major plus three minor; or (d) five minor. Major criteria are: typical organism in two or more separate blood cultures (or persistently positive) and evidence of endocardial involvement on echocardiography. Minor criteria include predisposition, fever, vascular phenomena, immunological phenomena, and microbiological evidence not meeting major. For IVDU tricuspid endocarditis, MSSA is most common; treatment is IV flucloxacillin 2 g four hourly for 2 to 6 weeks; TOE preferred over TTE for prosthetic valves and unclear TTE.
key_points: Duke: 2 majors, or 1 major + 3 minors, or 5 minors = definite.
IVDU tricuspid endocarditis most commonly MSSA.
Flucloxacillin 2 g IV 4 hourly for MSSA endocarditis.
TOE preferred to TTE for prosthetic valves or negative TTE with high suspicion.
explanation.pearls: Duke definite endocarditis by 2 major criteria: any typical organism in 2 or more separate cultures plus vegetation on echo; do not need pathology for the definite label.

sources.label: BSAC Duke criteria and endocarditis guidelines

stem:
A 68-year-old man presents to ED with a two-day history of severe headache, vomiting and fever, brought in by his wife. He has been progressively drowsy over the last six hours. He is a heavy smoker with COPD and has diet-controlled type 2 diabetes.

On arrival his GCS is 12 (E3 V4 M5). He has neck stiffness and a positive Kernig's sign. He has no focal neurological deficit. His pupils are equal at 3 mm and briskly reactive. There is no petechial rash.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118/min, blood pressure 92/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 95 percent on room air, temperature 39.2 degrees C
data_table.Examination: GCS 12; neck stiffness; Kernig positive; no focal deficit; no papilloedema on fundoscopy; no petechiae
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22.4 x10^9/L, CRP 340 mg/L (below 5); coags within normal limits; blood glucose 8.4 mmol/L; blood cultures taken

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate treatment before lumbar puncture?

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone 2 g and vancomycin 25 mg/kg targeting community meningitis pathogens
options.rationale: Missing benzylpenicillin misses Listeria cover which is essential above age 50 or in immunocompromised patients. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin 2.4 g and gentamicin 5 mg/kg empirically for suspected bacterial meningitis
options.rationale: This regimen misses ceftriaxone or cefotaxime which are cornerstone empiric cover for pneumococcal meningitis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous cefotaxime 2 g and metronidazole 500 mg targeting anaerobic and gram-negative cover
options.rationale: Metronidazole is not required for community meningitis and misses Listeria; benzylpenicillin plus a third generation cephalosporin is standard. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Intravenous dexamethasone 10 mg then ceftriaxone 2 g plus benzylpenicillin 2.4 g four hourly
options.rationale: eTG empiric bacterial meningitis above age 50: dexamethasone 10 mg with or before first antibiotic dose, then ceftriaxone plus benzylpenicillin (Listeria cover). (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Wait for lumbar puncture and CT brain results before starting empirical antibiotic therapy
options.rationale: Antibiotics should not be delayed beyond 30 minutes for imaging or LP when meningitis is suspected; give empirically then image. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Empiric adult bacterial meningitis therapy in Australia is dexamethasone 10 mg IV before or with the first antibiotic dose, ceftriaxone 2 g IV twice daily (or cefotaxime 2 g IV six hourly) for pneumococcal and meningococcal cover, plus benzylpenicillin 2.4 g IV four hourly for Listeria cover in patients over 50, immunocompromised, or with alcohol use. If suspected penicillin-resistant pneumococcus, add vancomycin 25 to 30 mg/kg. Dexamethasone reduces neurological sequelae and mortality in pneumococcal meningitis. LP should not delay antibiotics; CT before LP only if focal deficit, GCS reduction, seizure, or immunocompromise.
key_points: Empiric therapy above age 50: ceftriaxone plus benzylpenicillin plus dexamethasone.
Vancomycin added if penicillin-resistant pneumococcus suspected.
Dexamethasone before or with first antibiotic dose.
Do not delay antibiotics for imaging or LP.
explanation.pearls: Empiric adult meningitis above age 50: dexamethasone 10 mg IV, ceftriaxone 2 g IV BD, plus benzylpenicillin 2.4 g IV four hourly for Listeria cover.
